title: The British library
titleCn: 大英图书馆应对科技变革

paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

We're thinking today, then, about the impact of the rapid technological changes on society and public services. In this lecture, I want to consider the impact these changes are having on modern library services. What are the needs and expectations of customers using such a range of information services these days?

For this lecture, I'm going to use the British Library in London as a model. In order to cope with computer age changes, this library has introduced what it calls a market-facing approach. It's done that by identifying firstly its customer groups, researchers, businesses, the information sector, learners like you, and the general public, then finding ways to ensure its services are aligned with the needs of these five key customer groups. How do you go about identifying these needs? Well, the institution can only do that by conducting market research, and it's gone about this in three different ways. The library's asked its visitors how satisfied they are with services and resources. Another thing it's done is set up focus groups selected from small and medium-sized enterprises in the scientific and creative industries. Thirdly, it carries out regular satisfaction surveys among customers who order documents from the library online.

But there's no point in finding out what's needed if you don't act on those findings. Predictably, people nowadays want more information, and they want it more quickly, so there's a huge move away from traditional postal services.

Consider the million documents that users can order from the library via email these days. Think of how long this service would have taken in the past. Find the document in the archives, copy it, post it.

With the new systems in place at the library, once a document is ordered, it takes less than two hours for it to be delivered to a user's desktop. You'd have been lucky to receive it within five days with the old system, but today's customers would find this unacceptable. But there are problems with providing this kind of electronic resource. The collection of material is the prime concern. The library needs to implement effective systems and policies to make sure its resources are both relevant content-wise and as broadly accessible as possible. To achieve this, they're planning to build a digital store that will take a whole range of material. The scale of this operation is huge, and as I said, there'll be lots of problems to resolve. Another concern is how to ensure the preservation of material for decades, even centuries to come, and there are no off-the-shelf solutions. But the British Library, working in conjunction with others, hopes to come up with an answer.

But the challenges for libraries aren't only concerned with digitization and long-term preservation. It's not just about deciding what to digitize and then getting on with creating digital images and holding them all on file. Once you've got the basic content that users need, you need to think about adding attachments and creating links for users to access further related material. It's a huge project.

So I think you're beginning to understand that modern libraries are no longer going to be that quiet place you drove to in order to pick out a few books staffed by kind ladies in spectacles. There's going to be a lot more going on behind the scenes.

Talking of staff, it's going to be important for existing library staff to develop new core skills, too. So libraries are organizing skill programs to achieve that aim. There'll obviously be a need to recruit staff, too. There'll be new job titles and new areas of expertise needed. People with good marketing skills, for example, to target key customer groups as effectively as possible.

Now, many of you, I know, are thinking about working in library services once you've graduated. So my last point for you to consider before we move on today is this. If technology is going to make knowledge freely available to the many and not just the few, will there still be a need for librarians in the future?

Be reassured that many of the traditional roles performed by librarians are still and will continue to be important in the e-world. Librarians will be trained to help users find what they need using the same traditional three-stage approach they used in order to find information in books. That's selection and acquisition of the resource from the mass that is available, then identification of the information needed.

Librarians of the future will need hybrid skills. By that, I mean librarians are going to have to have a broader skills base. Perhaps we should offer a new degree course to meet those needs. You could study for a degree in library science, perhaps. You'd need to develop skills in IT and computer science as well as the more traditional literature and sociology.
Well, I'll look forward to hearing the English literature undergraduates' views on that in seminars next week. Right. Now let's move on to the question...
That is the end of Part Four. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part Four.
